C0.quote: This paper investigates the manipulative power of the polling agency.
C0.note: Iterative voting under plurality and veto; strategic and computational aspects of manipulation.

C1.quote: Several restricted variants are considered with respect to their parameterized complexity.
C1.note: Most results are hardness and FPT/P results; heuristics tested by simulation (impartial culture). Manipulation by the polling agency is also a strategic-behaviour problem.

C2.1.quote: each voter i is asked to submit a ballot

C2.2.quote: ballot bi ∈ M corresponding to a single candidate
C2.2.note: Single-candidate ballot: plurality vote or veto vote. Not an approval set in the codebook's sense, so coded OTH.

C2.3.quote: Each voter i has strict ordinal preferences over the candidates

C2.4.quote: A profile of ballots is said to be truthful if each agent submits
C2.4.note: Ballots b_i and preferences are separate notation, and ballots may deviate from truthful ones.

C3.1.quote: We assume that the voters only deviate when they believe that they are pivotal
C3.1.note: All analyses involve voters deviating strategically according to beliefs. The initial profile is truthful but dynamics are strategic.

C3.2.quote: We assume that the initial profile b0 is truthful

C4.1.note: The paper does not use utility, welfare or distortion for voters. Only ordinal preferences.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Criteria are manipulation success frequency and complexity. Condorcet and Borda winners appear only as target candidates, not as evaluation of welfare.

VOT.quote_behav: every voter can update her ballot with respect to this information
VOT.quote_info: we assume that voters only have partial knowledge about the other ballots
VOT.note: Voters follow best-response or veto-winner deviations based on beliefs from the poll and neighbours.

ORG.quote_behav: Can the polling agency announce a plausible poll
ORG.quote_info: it is reasonable to assume complete information for the polling agency
ORG.note: The polling agency is coded as ORG (a chair-like actor who chooses the announced poll). It is the manipulator pursuing a constructive or destructive goal.

BRI.note: The polling agency could be seen as an external manipulator but is coded under ORG.

C7.1.note: Both voters and the polling agency are strategic.

C8.1.quote: While best response deviations are considered under plurality
C8.1.note: Voters follow iterative best-response dynamics; the polling agency's manipulation is studied as a decision problem.

C8.2.quote: We consider a strategic game called iterative voting

claims.quote: This is particularly important when considering real-world problems.
manipulating is easier for the polling agency, especially under veto.

C9.1.note: Claims about real-world relevance of the model and results.

C9.2.quote: voters may have a local information by their relatives in a social network
C9.2.note: The claims rely on which agents are strategic and what they know. Both are stated in the model.
